title: Dare to Lead
author: Brené Brown
thesisParagraph: Courageous leadership is not a personality trait or a heroic mood; it is a teachable set of behaviors for staying present in uncertainty, naming values, building trust, and recovering after failure. Work cultures become braver when leaders replace self-protective armor with clear language, boundaries, empathy, and accountable practice.

signatureMoves: mixes research language with kitchen-table confession and repair after shame
uses permission-giving second person without letting the reader off the hook
names vulnerability, armor, rumbling, and courage as lived practices
moves from personal disclosure to a teachable relational distinction
links research terms to plain workplace behaviors and meeting rituals
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not polish shame into abstract leadership vocabulary.
Do not make vulnerability sound soft, decorative, or consequence-free.
does not treat courage as innate charisma or title-based authority
does not use detached clinical distance when discussing shame or fear

voiceSpecimens: You don't need braver language first; you need one honest sentence you can stand behind.
Armor gets lighter when you name what you're protecting.
teachingArc: Part 1 establishes vulnerability as the nonnegotiable core skill and separates courage from oversharing, weakness, perfectionism, shame, and defensive armor. Part 2 turns values into observable behavior, Part 3 operationalizes trust through the BRAVING inventory, and Part 4 teaches the recovery process for emotional setbacks and failed attempts.
forbiddenMoves: Do not remove the self-implicating warmth from Brown-style teaching.
Do not turn courage into a poster slogan without a hard conversation attached.
